segments.heading: Introduction
segments.text: Schwannomas are typically benign, slow-growing tumors originating from Schwann cells of peripheral nerves that may cause neurological symptoms due to nerve compression.^(,)

segments.heading: Introduction
segments.text: Facial Nerve Schwannomas (FNS) are uncommon, and present with facial paralysis, hearing loss or a regional mass. Those arising in the intraparotid segment are extremely rare and often preserve facial nerve function. This case highlights the recurrence of an Intraparotid Facial Nerve Schwannoma (IFNS) with worsening clinical presentation after debulking, an aspect rarely addressed in current literature, and discusses diagnostic and therapeutic challenges.

segments.heading: Case report
segments.text: We present a case of a recurrent IFNS in a 58-year-old mixed-race Brazilian woman. The patient’s medical history included hypertension treated with propranolol and tubal ligation, with no other comorbidities, allergies, or drug use.

segments.heading: Case report
segments.text: The patient presented with isolated facial paralysis and was evaluated by an otolaryngologist at a regional public referral hospital. Physical examination revealed grade IV Peripheral Facial Paralysis (PFP) on the House-Brackmann scale. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed an expansile, contrast-enhancing lesion with diffusion restriction along the right facial nerve, with an intraparotid component measuring 1.9 × 1.6 × 1.5 cm (Fig. 1).
segments.text_with_reference_markers: The patient presented with isolated facial paralysis and was evaluated by an otolaryngologist at a regional public referral hospital. Physical examination revealed grade IV Peripheral Facial Paralysis (PFP) on the House-Brackmann scale. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed an expansile, contrast-enhancing lesion with diffusion restriction along the right facial nerve, with an intraparotid component measuring 1.9 × 1.6 × 1.5 cm ( [FIG:fig0005 Fig. 1] ).

segments.heading: Case report
segments.text: Fine-Needle Aspiration (FNA) of the intraparotid nodule was performed. Cytology showed fibromyxoid stroma with cells displaying scant cytoplasm, wavy nuclei with tapered ends and occasional intranuclear incursions. One mitotic figure and focal nuclear palisading were observed. Findings were consistent with schwannoma.

segments.heading: Case report
segments.text: Surgical management consisted of parotid tumour resection. A preauricular incision with cervical extension was performed, followed by elevation of skin flaps and exposure of the parotid gland. The main trunk of the facial nerve was not identified. A cystic lesion enveloping the facial nerve was visualized.

segments.heading: Case report
segments.text: Histopathological examination confirmed schwannoma. Due to the low reported recurrence of cranial schwannomas, tumor debulking with facial nerve preservation was performed. Intraoperatively, thinning of the facial nerve fibers was observed following lesion reduction. Microsurgical repair was performed, and hemostasis achieved.

segments.heading: Case report
segments.text: Postoperatively, the patient remained clinically stable with persistent grade IV PFP. Early wound evaluation was satisfactory, with unchanged PFP. Physiotherapy was initiated and lubricating eye drops were prescribed.

segments.heading: Case report
segments.text: Two years and eight months later, Computed Tomography (CT) revealed a lobulated nodular lesion in the right parotid space, with heterogeneous contrast enhancement and measuring 1.5 × 1.4 cm. The patient also reported local pain and worsening PFP, which had progressed to grade V on the House-Brackmann scale. Conservative management with clinical monitoring and analgesics was instituted.

segments.heading: Case report
segments.text: One and a half years later, paralysis progressed to grade VI. An MRI was requested, which was delayed 15-months because of limited access to specialized imaging. It demonstrated hypodense material in the right inner ear with extension to the parotid gland and similar characteristics to the prior study, with slight enlargement of the posterior parotid component measuring approximately 1.3 × 1.2 cm.

segments.heading: Case report
segments.text: Given these findings, complete tumor resection with hypoglossal-facial nerve anastomosis was planned for facial reanimation.

segments.heading: Discussion
segments.text: The behaviour of FNS is largely determined by tumor topography.^(1) Intratemporal lesions predominate and characteristically produce facial nerve dysfunction, whereas the rare extratemporal tumours involving the intraparotid segment usually present as parotid masses with preserved facial function. Although most IFNS are described as indolent and slow growing, this case demonstrates that those tumors may follow an aggressive trajectory that the prevailing literature does not adequately capture.

segments.heading: Discussion
segments.text: Diagnostic uncertainty reflects a limitation intrinsic to the entity. Cross-sectional imaging of cranial nerve schwannomas is frequently subtle and nonspecific, demanding clinicoradiologic correlation and detailed anatomical knowledge. MRI typically reveals heterogeneous T2 hyperintensity, low-to-intermediate T1 signal intensity and avid contrast enhancement. Although the “target sign” is considered specific for schwannoma, it is seldom observed in cranial-nerve tumors. Uncertainty is greater in intraparotid schwannomas, which usually present as circumscribed parotid masses and frequently mimic benign salivary neoplasms.

segments.heading: Discussion
segments.text: Cytological assessment is similarly constrained. Fine-needle aspiration of peripheral nerve sheath tumours yields heterogeneous, frequently nonspecific findings that overlap with other spindle-cell neoplasms, while degenerative atypia may simulate malignancy and characteristic architectural features may be absent. Cytology is therefore prone to nondiagnostic or equivocal results, and ancillary immunohistochemistry is often required for definitive classification.

segments.heading: Discussion
segments.text: The optimal surgical management of IFNS remains non-consensual because treatment must balance oncologic control with preservation of facial nerve function, a decision compounded by the frequent absence of definitive preoperative diagnosis.^(,) Radiologic surveillance is therefore limited to select patients, particularly elderly individuals in whom a confident diagnosis can be established.

[BIBR:bib0010 2] , [BIBR:bib0025 5] Radiologic surveillance is therefore limited to select patients, particularly elderly individuals in whom a confident diagnosis can be established. segments.heading: Discussion
segments.text: When surgery is undertaken, total resection is advocated when facial movement is already poor or the nerve cannot be preserved, mandating reconstruction. Nerve-sparing subtotal techniques are appropriate only when intraoperative findings permit fascicular preservation and are associated with superior functional outcomes.^(,)

segments.heading: Discussion
segments.text: This case highlights the limitations of nerve-preserving surgery in patients with advanced facial dysfunction. Subtotal nerve-sparing resection was followed by recurrence within 3-years, pain, and paralysis progression, ultimately requiring complete resection with hypoglossal-facial anastomosis. The conservative strategy therefore did not prevent progression and arguably delayed definitive treatment.

segments.heading: Discussion
segments.text: Such an outcome is particularly instructive given the low reported recurrence rate of IFNS 2.38% (one patient in a 17-year cohort). The scarcity of documented recurrences makes the present case a meaningful illustration of treatment failure after initial nerve-preserving surgery, and supports a lower threshold for early radical resection in patients with substantial facial dysfunction.

segments.heading: Conclusion
segments.text: IFNS remains a rare entity associated with diagnostic uncertainty and complex therapeutic decision-making. This case illustrates that recurrence with progressive facial dysfunction may occur despite initial nerve-preserving management, underscoring the limitations of conservative or subtotal approaches in selected patients.

segments.heading: Conclusion
segments.text: Careful clinicoradiologic evaluation and individualized surgical planning are therefore essential to optimize functional outcomes. These findings provide meaningful clinical insight to the limited literature on recurrent IFNS and its management.

text:
[b00001] Introduction
Schwannomas are typically benign, slow-growing tumors originating from Schwann cells of peripheral nerves that may cause neurological symptoms due to nerve compression.^(,)

[b00002] Introduction
Facial Nerve Schwannomas (FNS) are uncommon, and present with facial paralysis, hearing loss or a regional mass. Those arising in the intraparotid segment are extremely rare and often preserve facial nerve function. This case highlights the recurrence of an Intraparotid Facial Nerve Schwannoma (IFNS) with worsening clinical presentation after debulking, an aspect rarely addressed in current literature, and discusses diagnostic and therapeutic challenges.

[b00003] Case report
We present a case of a recurrent IFNS in a 58-year-old mixed-race Brazilian woman. The patient’s medical history included hypertension treated with propranolol and tubal ligation, with no other comorbidities, allergies, or drug use.

[b00004] Case report
The patient presented with isolated facial paralysis and was evaluated by an otolaryngologist at a regional public referral hospital. Physical examination revealed grade IV Peripheral Facial Paralysis (PFP) on the House-Brackmann scale. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed an expansile, contrast-enhancing lesion with diffusion restriction along the right facial nerve, with an intraparotid component measuring 1.9 × 1.6 × 1.5 cm (Fig. 1).

[b00005] Case report
Fine-Needle Aspiration (FNA) of the intraparotid nodule was performed. Cytology showed fibromyxoid stroma with cells displaying scant cytoplasm, wavy nuclei with tapered ends and occasional intranuclear incursions. One mitotic figure and focal nuclear palisading were observed. Findings were consistent with schwannoma.

[b00006] Case report
Surgical management consisted of parotid tumour resection. A preauricular incision with cervical extension was performed, followed by elevation of skin flaps and exposure of the parotid gland. The main trunk of the facial nerve was not identified. A cystic lesion enveloping the facial nerve was visualized.

[b00007] Case report
Histopathological examination confirmed schwannoma. Due to the low reported recurrence of cranial schwannomas, tumor debulking with facial nerve preservation was performed. Intraoperatively, thinning of the facial nerve fibers was observed following lesion reduction. Microsurgical repair was performed, and hemostasis achieved.

[b00008] Case report
Postoperatively, the patient remained clinically stable with persistent grade IV PFP. Early wound evaluation was satisfactory, with unchanged PFP. Physiotherapy was initiated and lubricating eye drops were prescribed.

[b00009] Case report
Two years and eight months later, Computed Tomography (CT) revealed a lobulated nodular lesion in the right parotid space, with heterogeneous contrast enhancement and measuring 1.5 × 1.4 cm. The patient also reported local pain and worsening PFP, which had progressed to grade V on the House-Brackmann scale. Conservative management with clinical monitoring and analgesics was instituted.

[b00010] Case report
One and a half years later, paralysis progressed to grade VI. An MRI was requested, which was delayed 15-months because of limited access to specialized imaging. It demonstrated hypodense material in the right inner ear with extension to the parotid gland and similar characteristics to the prior study, with slight enlargement of the posterior parotid component measuring approximately 1.3 × 1.2 cm.

[b00011] Case report
Given these findings, complete tumor resection with hypoglossal-facial nerve anastomosis was planned for facial reanimation.

[b00012] Discussion
The behaviour of FNS is largely determined by tumor topography.^(1) Intratemporal lesions predominate and characteristically produce facial nerve dysfunction, whereas the rare extratemporal tumours involving the intraparotid segment usually present as parotid masses with preserved facial function. Although most IFNS are described as indolent and slow growing, this case demonstrates that those tumors may follow an aggressive trajectory that the prevailing literature does not adequately capture.

[b00013] Discussion
Diagnostic uncertainty reflects a limitation intrinsic to the entity. Cross-sectional imaging of cranial nerve schwannomas is frequently subtle and nonspecific, demanding clinicoradiologic correlation and detailed anatomical knowledge. MRI typically reveals heterogeneous T2 hyperintensity, low-to-intermediate T1 signal intensity and avid contrast enhancement. Although the “target sign” is considered specific for schwannoma, it is seldom observed in cranial-nerve tumors. Uncertainty is greater in intraparotid schwannomas, which usually present as circumscribed parotid masses and frequently mimic benign salivary neoplasms.

[b00014] Discussion
Cytological assessment is similarly constrained. Fine-needle aspiration of peripheral nerve sheath tumours yields heterogeneous, frequently nonspecific findings that overlap with other spindle-cell neoplasms, while degenerative atypia may simulate malignancy and characteristic architectural features may be absent. Cytology is therefore prone to nondiagnostic or equivocal results, and ancillary immunohistochemistry is often required for definitive classification.

[b00015] Discussion
The optimal surgical management of IFNS remains non-consensual because treatment must balance oncologic control with preservation of facial nerve function, a decision compounded by the frequent absence of definitive preoperative diagnosis.^(,) Radiologic surveillance is therefore limited to select patients, particularly elderly individuals in whom a confident diagnosis can be established.

[b00016] Discussion
When surgery is undertaken, total resection is advocated when facial movement is already poor or the nerve cannot be preserved, mandating reconstruction. Nerve-sparing subtotal techniques are appropriate only when intraoperative findings permit fascicular preservation and are associated with superior functional outcomes.^(,)

[b00017] Discussion
This case highlights the limitations of nerve-preserving surgery in patients with advanced facial dysfunction. Subtotal nerve-sparing resection was followed by recurrence within 3-years, pain, and paralysis progression, ultimately requiring complete resection with hypoglossal-facial anastomosis. The conservative strategy therefore did not prevent progression and arguably delayed definitive treatment.

[b00018] Discussion
Such an outcome is particularly instructive given the low reported recurrence rate of IFNS 2.38% (one patient in a 17-year cohort). The scarcity of documented recurrences makes the present case a meaningful illustration of treatment failure after initial nerve-preserving surgery, and supports a lower threshold for early radical resection in patients with substantial facial dysfunction.

[b00019] Conclusion
IFNS remains a rare entity associated with diagnostic uncertainty and complex therapeutic decision-making. This case illustrates that recurrence with progressive facial dysfunction may occur despite initial nerve-preserving management, underscoring the limitations of conservative or subtotal approaches in selected patients.

[b00020] Conclusion
Careful clinicoradiologic evaluation and individualized surgical planning are therefore essential to optimize functional outcomes. These findings provide meaningful clinical insight to the limited literature on recurrent IFNS and its management.
